segments.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to this special session called SMR Deployment Readiness.

My name is Wei Huang, the Director for Planning, Information, and Knowledge Management of IAEA. It's my great honor to come back to this very important global gathering because last year I was here. I think the people who were here last year, you can agree with me that last year already quite successful, impactful, and this year even more successful, impactful up to today.

So it's my great pleasure to be here and I would like to take a chance to thank the Rwanda host, the government, and the Rwanda Atomic Energy Board for inviting agencies to contribute to this important global dialogue. And you see from yesterday, our DG Grossi delivered this very important In-Ear Missions Phase One to the Rwanda National President and also signed an MOU with the Infrastructure Minister of Rwanda, which demonstrates that agency's strong commitment to support Rwanda's ambition to go nuclear in the coming decade. For this session, I think we are going to have a deep dive on the SMR Deployment Readiness because I think it's a very interesting topic.
A lot of people want to know what global status is. May I? Oh, sorry, yes. So, which should I point to? Is that correct for the bottom? I need some technical assistance.

Yeah, while I'm waiting for this issue to be resolved, I would like to also mention that when we look at this African continent, it is sustainable industrialization, digital transformation, and the universal access to affordable energy has never been more urgent. So, when we notice that about 600 million people lack access to reliable energy. Even now, renewables are playing the vital piece in the energy metrics, but it cannot solve the problem alone.

They need some other sources. So, nuclear can really provide this kind of a reliable, low-carbon energy basal option to support African continent transition. Can I have my slides on again? Okay, let me start from this one.

You can see, it has been mentioned already in the previous speakers yesterday, and talking about a global strong momentum established especially since the COP28. And this is a very important occasion that nuclear first time was included in the global stocktake document, which is the official document of UNFCCC under the Paris Agreement. And also, this momentum has been strengthened and boosted and accelerated by the following events, including the first Nuclear Energy Summit in 2024, and also this March, the second Nuclear Energy Summit in Paris.

And so, I think so, in order to keep this one, I think I want to reflect what we are, we stand today in terms of the global nuclear status. You can see from these slides, we have about 415 reactors in operation in 31 countries, and 72 under construction. This number keep changing, just bear in mind.

The next day, you will see a different number because you see a lot of investment and projects ongoing. So, you can see there's a global tendency regarding how many countries are interested in addition to the 31 operating countries, 42 newcomers, which agencies are listed, including the host country, Rwanda, and also other African countries who have strong interest in nuclear to support their energy transition. But if you look at the agencies, this is a very important global projection of nuclear energy by 2050.

You can see this is also a very positive tendency regarding nuclear energy by 2050. So, the last year, 2025 addition reflects both high-case and low-case projection increase. This is actually the fifth consecutive year regarding this increased tendency.

Among this information, I also want to mention that this conference is very much focused on this SMR potential contribution. So, we see SMR will play a very essential role in the high-case projection of agency assessment, especially after 2030. So, I think there has been already mentioned about why SMR is interested by so many countries.

I don't want to go into the details of this one, but I think these are the main attributes regarding why SMR is getting more and more interest from the countries, both operating countries, developed economies, and also emerging markets. So, you see a nuclear SMR can really provide some kind of cost affordability to the country, especially for newcomer countries because they can have a chance to lower the upfront cost. It has been already highlighted by the countries' leaders yesterday, they can also have this very unique advantage in terms of modularization. They can have a simplified design. They can also have some multiple modules.

We can have some flexibility to contribute to the different needs. And so, they can also have some options to work with renewable energy to create some kind of a hybrid system to support this global transition together. So, look at this chart.

You can see how the interest in the SMR increased in the past decade. You can see on the left side, this is actually about the vendor side, how many different designs have increased in the past 10 years. I will just give the number up to 2022.
Actually, from 2022 to today, the number also increased. You heard the previous speaker talk about 100 different designs, 120 different designs. Yeah, that's reflected interest on the design side.

But talking about the demand side, you can see also the number increased in the past six years from interest, one country interest, SMR, and growing to today's more than 25. So, you see the both, and I see the very strong interest in SMR. Regarding agency's information about the global SMR status, we keep tracking the global development in terms of designs, and our 2024 catalog, SMR catalog, capture active design of SMR among more than 100 different designs, because we try to not dilute our focus, because we have some kind of a methodology applied for country to see which technology are really move forward, which actually has been slowed down or even stopped.

And also, we are working on our new version, 2026 version, and talking about SMR, the latest SMR status at global level. So, you can see from the 2024 catalog, we have this category reflect different kind of technologies in terms of what neutron they are using, fast neutron or thermal neutron, or use what kind of a coolant, light water or gas, or different technology, and even very innovative technology from these micro-reactors. So, talking about how we define the different stages, agency try to be not biased.

We try to use some methodology to apply to different design and to assess their readiness, their stages. That is why we use this kind of layers to define different design and the different readiness of the technologies, from the concept description down to this operation status. So, based on that, you can see this is the 2024 catalog, the global status in terms of their readiness.

But this is already outdated. I just give some kind of a reflection about how agencies use a methodology to reflect the status of global SMR development. Actually, I want to also draw your attention to this one, so this is more current status of global SMR.
So, you can see only two SMR in operation. This one is in Russia. It's a floating reactor.
The second one is a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor. Both are already in operation for more than three years. A floating reactor even longer than the high-temperature gas-cooled reactor.

And in terms of the SMR and the construction, you can see there we have seven different designs from a carrying in Argentina to natural, which has just got a construction permit in the US. Now it's already under construction this year. And the Aurora is also very fast track, on the very fast track, which is under construction in the Idaho National Labs, supported by the US.
And also BWRX, which is using the boiling water technologies. It's also quite advanced. They are building this one in Canada.

And also RITM-200 technology, which is a Russian-type land-based SMR. And also the BRASS-OD-300, which is also a very innovative concept to put all these closed-fuel cycle systems. And now it's also under construction, and move quite advanced stage.

And last but not least, ASB-100. This is a Chinese design, 100 megawatt, in the Hainan Nuclear Power Plant, Changjiang Nuclear Power Plant, which is very close to the operation by the end of this year. In addition to that one, there are the two designs also very close to their construction, which one is X-Energy, XC-100, and also EVEN-G technology from Westinghouse.

And then they have the other one, two, three, four, I think it's four technology, which also will be kick-off very soon. And then it will be put into construction after 2030, given the current preparation of each project. So when we look at this very promising status of the SMR, we also realize that in order to make SMR can be really available and feasible in the market, we still need to talk about some issues around SMRs.

So we need more demonstrations, especially for those very innovative technologies, to make sure the first of the kind will be deployed quickly. And also we need to make sure they have a continuous order to make, because SMR, given the size, they have some kind of a challenge in terms of economic competitiveness. So we need to keep the order of the SMR by building more and improve the economic value of the SMR.

And also regulatory framework, because traditionally the SMR is much, most, we don't have a very specific regulatory guidance framework, address SMR. We use the large-scale reactor system, regulatory system to cover the SMR technology. But given the very innovative ideas and some kind of special features, we need some kind of improved regulatory system to address its special needs.

And also we need to build up some infrastructure, which our agency has been working with the member states to prepare for their infrastructure aspect, covering lighting issues. So yesterday, this in-air mission report actually also can relate to this effort. So this is, I just quickly go through this one.

You saw how agencies support member states in terms of information, in terms of capacity building, in terms of building a strong and adaptive legislation framework. And also talking about how nuclear has some kind of issues to be taken into account when the country starts to build SMR in terms of the safety, security, even safeguards. And also radioactive waste.

So milestone approach, I'm not going to go into that detail because given the time I have, but I think I suggest you look at our agency website to see how the actual agency will support the member state needs in terms of also lighting issues related to the first nuclear program in the country. And also the Auto for Net Zero is one of the efforts agencies try to help countries to build up a long-term plan to position nuclear energy in their long-term energy planning and also energy strategy. And also this is another example, NYSE is also initially launched by the agency, trying to streamline the current legislation, regulatory framework to facilitate the SMR development and also deployment.

And also this is a very important platform. I strongly recommend you to go there to see how many activities the agency conducted to support the specific needs of the country in terms of SMR. From different design, from different services, from the capacity building, we also have SMR school now running in different continent, including Africa.

And now we have to be also sober about the challenges we are facing when we see the very promising future of nuclear, including SMR. We have to make sure all this issue will be taken into account, including what I already mentioned about licensing issues and how to prove the operability and the maintainability and also how to address this supply chain, which is also mentioned during this conference quite intensively. And also some non-technical issues we also need to address, including this kind of economic competitiveness and also availability of this offshore design for newcomers, how they're going to select.

So that is also one thing I want to mention, that agency, we have this technology review assisting the wide service to help countries to review the different vendor designs. This is also an additional service to the member states. So now let me turn to this objective of the panel.

So it's my great honor to invite our distinguished panel to come to the podium. Dr. Sama Bilbao y Leon, Director General for World Nuclear Association. And Mr. Nana Manya Ayensu, CEO of Zorro Energy Solution.

And also non-resident fellow at the Center of Global Energy Policy. And Dr. Fidel Ndahayo, CEO of Rwanda Atomic Energy Board. And Vilaphi Ntuli, the Chief Nuclear Officer of Eskom Koeberg Nuclear Power Plant.

Mr. Alexey Semenov, the Head for the Business Development ,advisor,ROSATOM Central and South Africa. And Mr. Rafael Marin, Director of Holtec Europe. And last but not least, Irfan Hasan, Managing Director of Bertin Technologies and the GIFEN Pilot Club Africa.
Okay, so we have one hour. We have a very well-known panelist. And so I will start from Dr.Sama.

What are your views regarding the most critical industry-led innovation that makes the SMR viable for the African utilities compared to large-scale reactors? Well, thank you, Wei, and thank you, obviously, to Rwanda for inviting me to be here and also the International Atomic Energy Agency for joining this session. I have to say, you're asking me a question that was almost answered in your presentation and in the previous short sketch that we have. So I will really not take a lot of time because you have here lots of people that are going to give you much more detail on specific reactor designs.

But maybe just a quick view. I think that small modular reactors and micro-reactors have been an excellent opportunity to open new doors for nuclear energy around the world. So I think that even countries or organizations that were not necessarily excited about nuclear energy, became very excited about the small modular reactors.

So I think that that's been a fabulous door opener and a great conversation starter for nuclear energy. So – and as you know, when we started designing small modular reactors, perhaps, well, probably 15, 20 years ago, there were – I mean, well, there were a few before that. But when we started to do this very seriously, it was probably because ,at the time, we felt that the market could not really bear very large reactors.

We were seeing lots of addition of variable, renewable energy. So we felt that smaller reactors were going to be better to manage loads and to manage flexibility. But in addition to that, I think that the key new thing that we tried to bring with nuclear reactors was a new delivery model.
Because you will see that technology – I mean, there are many technological advances. We are using advanced safety features. We have many interesting improvements and performance enhancements.

But I think that the big new thing is really the delivery mechanism. So we are going to have a reactor that is relatively small, that is going to be totally standardized, that is probably going to be modularized and or factory-fabricated, almost – maybe not in every case, but in many cases, almost you can put it on the back of a truck, on the back of a barge, and just ship it to wherever it is going to be deployed. And with minimum civil infrastructure, you can actually start operating.

So you are looking at much shorter construction times. Well, much more affordable units, because being smaller, well, the capital investment is going to be smaller. And you are going to see much more predictability in the entire process.

So I think that that's what really is going to make the SMR different versus the large reactors. And I think that these guys probably are going to give you much more details about the different nuances of different technologies. So maybe I'll stop here.

Thank you very much,Dr. Sama. You mentioned these very important attributes of the SMR and also how actually the nuclear industry, led by the WNA, supports these efforts collectively. I think that's very important, because innovation really can help to achieve this objective, which has been listed here, the modernization, standardization, and also delivering a model.
I think it's valuable to make these efforts. Thank you very muchDr, Sama. Nana, I turn to you.

What is actually the innovative financing structure? Because you have been in the government and also industry, you have very broad experience. So I'm very happy to listen to your views about this innovative financing structure and the risk-sharing model could make the SMR project in Africa bankable while ensuring the balance, the responsibility among the government, vendors, and the different stakeholder utilities and the different stakeholders. Sure.

Thank you so much, Wei. When I think about your question, I like to think about it in a few different ways. So as we know, and as Wei mentioned in his presentation, there are many unique benefits of nuclear energy.

Nuclear energy, both as an asset class and also just as a new solution, also creates some unique challenges when it comes to financing. So when you think about first of all, on a relative basis, the high balance of capex, especially up front, typically has longer construction times and then also a longer amortization period. Now, when it comes to structuring, I mean, structuring is not by itself an answer, but it's a way to strategically solve problems or to solve challenges with these.

And so stepping away from just traditional, oh, should it be ? Should you use Mancala? Just another way of thinking about it. I'll give you a couple examples, maybe three examples. So one is to not think about just one structure, but to try to deconstruct a nuclear project into its different phases.

Turn it into a three-dimensional problem. It's not just what structure do you need, but what kind of structure do you need at what stage of the projects and matched with what capital sources that have the risk appetite and also the balance to be able to support that. So if you start to break it up into, what kind of capital do you need to support early stage project developments? What kind of capital do you need to construct to support the construction phase? And also what kind of capital do you need to support long-term operations and so on? And you make it more of a relay race where it's not just one opportunity that's trying to balance a whole project, but it's you're handing off the opportunities and the risks and matching those along the entire course of development.

So you can have more high-risk capital, that's perhaps a bit more structure like equity for the earliest phases. And then bring in more, whereas once the plan is operating, bring in more lower risk, longer term, lower cost of capital, institutional capital to help bring down the cost of the project and to help provide that certainty. The second way in which I would think about it is from a commercial contracting standpoint.

So as many of you know, one of the biggest barriers, at least for most investors, for investing in new nuclear is the risk of cost and schedule overruns, particularly on construction. That is a known issue. I'd say nuclear has got a mixed history when it comes to that, but there are a lot of strategies that are useful to help to mitigate those things, everything from how you think about design, how you think about contracting.

But one in particular to your question is just to think about the integrated project delivery model as an example. There are different flavors of it. There's an example that's being implemented right now with the Darlington project in Canada.

But the way in which that works, instead of signing individual contracts between the owner and the EPC, the owner and the vendor, the owners and the offtakers, which can create misalignment. Classically, if there's, for instance, a delay in a project, that actually might be beneficial to the EPC, depending on if they have a traditional time and materials contract, because they make more money the longer the project goes, where that is, of course, at odds with the owner. But with an IPD, you basically get everybody under the same umbrella.

You create a shared profits pool between all the major entities. And with that, everybody gets paid and gets dispersed based on how well the project performed relative to a predetermined target. So if the project comes in at budget, you get the target compensation.

If it comes in below budget, all the counterparties make more. If the project comes in over budget, then that proper pool begins to shrink up until a maximum point. And that's a much stronger way of trying to drive commercial alignment and behavioral alignment as one that can help to put everybody on the same team, get everybody on the same page without trying to deploy.

Then the third thing that I would point out is just the importance of JVs. I think it's been talked about in a few panels, but it's not just about being a customer of nuclear, especially as Africans have the opportunity to own these projects, to own key parts of things. If you're going to be one of the first countries developing, and you're developing a new technology, and you're developing and you're taking the risk up front, it's helping to open up that market.

Entering into an agreement whereby you can share in the profits of future projects, perhaps with the vendor or with other projects and so on, could greatly be a de-risk. That provides another revenue stream on top of your on top of your project revenues. I think it's the last quick thing I'll say.
All of you have heard of the Mancala model. It's named after a town in Finland where this model was invented. I'm sure for anyone who's West African, probably think of Mancala as a different thing.
Mancala is a game. It's a strategy game that people play. This word, at least to me, I've heard so many times and always think of in its African context and not its Swedish context.

It's more so to say there's an opportunity to not just think about the Mancala model, but to come up with our own model. If you come a few down the line, what we see is the Kigali model, what we see is the Accra model, what we see is the Cairo model, what we see is the Kampala-Johannesburg model. Just some mix of things along the way that takes a lot of the things that exist, but fits them within the innovation context of Africa as well.

Thank you. Since you work, as I mentioned, in the government sector and also the industry sector, your insightful comments regarding how SMR can be deployed sustainably is valuable, especially talking about the structure approach and the integrated approach and even the ownership to make sure that African countries can run sustainably for the future in terms of energy development. Thank you very much for your comments.
Let me turn to our host, Dr. Ndahayo. You are the CEO of the Rwanda Atomic Energy Board. We just signed this MOU, and you completed the first phase of the engineering mission successfully.

Congratulations. What lessons have you learned from Rwanda's phase one engineering mission? Can you inform me of the broader African readiness for SMR? Thank you very much. First of all, let me recognize in the audience the presence of Mr. Mehmet from the IAEA, who was the leading expert that coordinated that engineering mission that was conducted in Rwanda in March this year.

Many in the audience may be familiar with the milestones approach promoted by the International Atomic Energy Agency, but for those who are not familiar, this is a wide-range assessment of the country's readiness to embark on a nuclear power program. The assessment is conducted – the scope is very wide, from national position to legal and regulatory framework, nuclear safety, nuclear security, electrical grid, radiation protection, environment protection, to procurement. And those are in total 19 issues that are assessed, and the assessment has been conducted based on the self-evaluation report that the country prepared itself before.

And from that assessment, Rwanda has done very well. Among the 19 issues, we have completed all the activities planned in phase one. Some work is meant to be done on three issues regarding human resource development, because at the beginning, we focused actually on projects that were promoted, meaning the SMR project and the research reactor project, and we forgot to consider the industry, the regulator.

So for this, we need now to elaborate comprehensive human resource development that cater for all the needs of the country. So another issue was actually stakeholder engagement. We have been doing some activities on this issue, but they were judged as sporadic activities because we did not have any strategy that was followed.

So now we are doing this one to make sure that we have a clear strategy that will inform our stakeholder engagement activities. The last one was industrial involvement, and that has been actually the main topic in previous sessions. And actually, so we have conducted a small assessment of the manufacturing capabilities in the country.

We didn't do the comprehensive assessment. Thankfully, now that has been completed, and we have all the ground data that is required to elaborate a viable strategy, because now the understanding is not only restricted to industry involvement during the implementation of the nuclear program, but I think in parallel, we need to elaborate an industrialization strategy of the whole country to make sure that the nuclear power program can actually boost the economic growth, the development, the economic growth that the country is willing to achieve. So mainly, they also, I think, pointed to best practices that can help other countries in the same situation.

I can just have one of them, because the time is somehow limited. So the best practices that I want to talk about is that, you know, all newcomers, when you start talking about nuclear energy, the fear is about what if an accident happens? What will happen? Are you ready to have some response? And on this topic, I think Rwanda has done a lot. We have what we call Rwanda's national nuclear and radiological emergency preparedness and response plan that includes emergency preparedness and response arrangements for nuclear installations, and it is already in existence.

It is being exercised. Sometimes we conduct some simulations to see if all involved people respond as planned. So without taking much time, I think that's what I can point out from the assessment that has been conducted.

I again take this opportunity to thank all the people that were involved. On our side, it was not on the Rwanda Atomic Energy Board. It was the Ministers Preparedness, the police, different security organs, the Rwanda environment.

So all institutions that were involved during the production of this energy emission are recognized. Thank you. Thank you very much, Dr. Ndahayo, for sharing this very detailed information regarding the energy emission report.

Usually we will wait for the green light from the host country to release that content. Are you down this way in the audience? I think this really reflects your transparency attitude during this important dialogue. Thank you very much for sharing that.

Let me turn to another important panelist from South Africa. Mr. Ntuli, South Africa is the only country in the continent running nuclear power plants. So given your experience, what unique challenges and opportunities do you see in developing SMRs? Last year, South Africa hosted a G20 presidency.

We work a lot with South Africa on how we can help your country to transfer from coal to nuclear, talking about aging coal power plants. But that also reflects your strong interest in deploying SMRs in the coming years. Please share your experience in this regard.

Thank you. And once again, congratulations to Dr. Ndahayo and the people of Rwanda for achieving such a wonderful milestone. As an operator of a nuclear power plant in the continent, we really want more and more countries in the continent to adopt nuclear technology because it really increases capacity in the continent.

So coming back to your question, the reason for South Africa pursuing SMRs is a bit different to what other countries might be pursuing. So just to give you an idea, currently South Africa has about 62 gigawatts of installed capacity. 46 of those belong to ESCOM.
In the next 10 years, we foresee that 9 gigawatts of that will be retired. So those are old and aging coal plants that we need to retire. So we have an opportunity then to address that energy gap.

And through our ministry, an integrated resource plan was pronounced. So the integrated resource plan really tells the energy plan for the country over the next 10 years. As part of that, 5.2 gigawatts of nuclear has been allocated in this integrated resource plan.

What do you plan to do with that and what the opportunities are? As you rightly say, during the G20 presidency, one of the key things to how we could address the retiring coal-fired plants was through SMRs. And why SMRs? SMRs are a technology that would be suitable where we have coal-fired power plants because they are inland. They are not in the coastal areas.

In the coastal areas, we deploy more large reactors. So this became a viable option for us that inland coal-fired power stations will then deploy SMRs. And the key advantages of that with the study that we did, we saw that with deployment of SMRs in those applications, we save up to 30% in cost, infrastructure cost, because you can use some of the infrastructure that you had for coal-fired power plants.

But the other key and attractive factor for us is we have this just transition. And the transition to a low-carbon economy, it cannot be just if it puts people out of work. And with the study that was done, it was clear that about 75% of the coal-fired power plants can be transitioned to become nuclear power plants.

Then the other opportunity that we see is really meaningful localization. So we speak about localization in these forums, but it has to be meaningful. So having to supply concrete and cement during the construction and then after there is no further jobs is really not localization.

So if we are going to replace about nine gigawatts of coal-fired power plants, we really need to say, what are we buying? Are we buying a product or are we buying a value chain? And as Africans, we really need to lean towards buying the whole value chain rather than buying a product. So that then translates to a meaningful localization, you know, and adoption of the technology. The other aspect of it, working closely with the other state entity, which is NEISA, is around fuel manufacturing.

We do have a facility in the African continent. And with this strategy, as we move forward with the 5.2 gigawatts, we need to push for the fuel to be manufactured in the African continent. There is absolutely no reason why we cannot do it at NEISA in South Africa.

And that's what the opportunities that we're looking at. When I get to the challenges part of it, some of the challenges that we face would be similar to countries that are adopting nuclear energy. We do have regulation and it's a mature regulation, but unfortunately, that regulation was for large reactors.
So we are in the process of adopting it for small modular reactors. As you have seen, maybe in the U.S. that, you know, regulation needs to be there. It's important.
The regulator needs to be independent. However, we need to have efficient and effective regulation. So we cannot frustrate the deployment of SMR by having a very bureaucratic regulation.

The other key challenge that we are facing in South Africa, we are retiring the plants in the next 10 years. And the key challenge, though, is how do we balance the risk of early adoption with the cost overruns, with the need for fast deployment? Because, you know, with any project that you do in the early phases, there's cost overruns, there's lessons learned that are going to happen, and those cost a lot of money. So we have to balance the need for speed of deployment and cost overrun.

And the last one that I'll leave with you for now is really the work that we still need to do around community acceptance and public acceptance. So there's a lot of work that we are going to do. Even with a country like ours, which is South Africa, over 60 years of nuclear experience, community acceptance is still a challenge that we need to continuously work on.
Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Ntuli. You gave a very comprehensive reflection regarding the perspective of South Africa in terms of nuclear energy.

You talk about a very important issue, like a just transition. And also we have some key issues regarding the UNFCCC climate change activation agenda of COP 30. And also you talk about the value chain establishment.

That is also a very important one, which actually has been intensively discussed in the past days, and also a morning session. And of course, some other issues that should be addressed during this facilitation of the nuclear deployment. Thank you very much for your point.
So let me turn to Mr. Wei, the Vice President of CNC. China is leading the new booth in the world. So based on the CNC's global experience, you also have an overseas project in Pakistan.

So what lessons can Africa draw in building the enabling infrastructure, including regulatory, and also the industry and human capacity to accelerate SMR deployment readiness? Okay, thank you. This is, I think, a very practical question. And from CNC's experience, I think there are three very important areas for Africa to focus on in order to support the future SMR deployment.

First, I think on the regulatory side, a stable and independent nuclear regulatory system is very important. Nuclear projects are long-term projects. Investors and the technical suppliers need clear regulation and a predictable licensing process.

For countries that are starting nuclear programs, I think cooperation with IAEA is also very important. Because IAEA can provide standards training and review services that can help countries to build confidence and improve safety systems. Actually, when China developed the SCP-100 technology, we also worked closely with IAEA.
In the year 2016, we applied for the GIS review for the SCP-100. And second, I think industrial capability is very essential. SMRs are smaller than the traditional nuclear power plants.

But they still require a strong infrastructure, local manufacturing capacity, and transportation, and et cetera. In CNC's overseas project, we learned that localization should be developed step by step. At the very beginning, more support may come from the international suppliers.

But over time, local companies can participate more in civil construction, equipment supply, maintenance, and other services. This helps reduce the cost and also will create local economic benefits. And the third is human resource development.

I think this is probably the most important foundation. Nuclear energy needs qualified engineers, operators, regulators, and technicians. Actually, CNC has a lot of experience cooperating with universities, research institutes, and training centers in different countries.

We believe that talent development should start as early as possible, even before the project construction begins. And SMR deployment is not only about technology. It's about building a complete ecosystem.

This includes policy support, financing, supply chains, education, regulation, and international cooperation. I think if these elements develop together, Africa has a strong potential to become a very important market for SMRs in the near future. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Mr. Wei, and mentioning these issues related to the independent regulatory system and also this localization issue has been also mentioned by the previous speakers already. Thank you. And also, thank you for mentioning the agency's support to your country's capacity.

And let me turn to Mr. Simenov, the head of the business of development of the advisor to ROSATOM. So, what is Rosatom's timeline for commercial SMR deployment in Africa? Because ROSATOM has a lot of different designs captured by the agency catalog. So, how do you plan to mitigate the financing risk? Thank you for the question.

So, in order to give you a proper answer, I would like to highlight several things, several points where we as Rosatom, as vendors, technology carriers stand and under which global environment we operate now. Let's take our first SMR export contract, for example, the US-Pakistan. The first EPC was signed in 2024, and the first criticality is expected by late 2029.

So, once the NPP is fully operational, the plant will generate close to 7.5 billion kilowatts per year and meet almost 14.4% of the demand, which is a huge benefit to the energy mix and the balance of the country. So, we as Rosatom currently have 41 units in 11 countries in our international portfolio, with 26 large units and two SMRs in active implementation across nine countries. So, Africa is an active member.
